newsitem.title: USA: White House urges FCC to hold off on TV rules.
newsitem.headline: White House urges FCC to hold off on TV rules.

text.p: The Clinton administration on Thursday urged the Federal Communications Commission to shelve indefinitely its proposal to ease rules governing the number of local television stations a media company can own.

Instead, the administration asked the FCC to first study the impact on competition and diversity that already have resulted from last year's communications law -- as well as the upcoming impact of high-definition digital TV.
The Commerce Department, in a filing with the FCC, also urged the FCC to strengthen its "attribution rules" which determine whether a person or company "owns" a broadcast station.

"To preserve competition and diversity, it is critical that we have effective ownership and attribution rules that do not allow media outlets to be held in fewer and fewer hands," Assistant Commerce Secretary Larry Irving said in a statement.
"We should make sure we fully understand what is happening in the marketplace before we further loosen the ownership rules," Irving said.
He added that since last year's communications law, "we have already seen profound changes and we can expect further changes during the conversion to digital broadcasting."
The administration's filing contended that loosening the ownership rules could result in minorities owning fewer and fewer media outlets.

"If history holds true, we can expect that a relaxation of media ownership rules will increase the demand for broadcast properties and that the principal beneficiaries will be those with sufficient capital to finance acquisition of increasingly expensive properties," said Irving.

The FCC proposal is intended to update the agency's rules after last year's communications law. The FCC proposed to allow common ownership of TV stations that are in separate designated market areas and that do not have overlapping "Grade A" contours, or signals that extend 50 to 70 miles.
Current FCC rules bar a media company from having interests in two TV stations whose "Grade B" signal countours overlap. Grade B refers to signals that extend 30 to 45 miles.
